newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-OPEC ENDS WITH NEW VOW TO CURB EXCESS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OPEC ENDS WITH NEW VOW TO CURB EXCESS.

text.p: OPEC ended Vienna talks on Thursday with a new freeze on its production limits, but whether the accord ratchets oil prices higher will depend on the cartel honouring vows to curb endemic violations.
Prices had ticked briskly up on Wednesday's news that the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries had struck a deal to "roll over" the current output ceiling to year's end.
But the market was several cents easier on Thursday, just above $18 for August Brent futures, by the time OPEC ended its conference and formally endorsed the deal.
Sceptical analysts argued that, longer term, the market would demand proof of what OPEC said were fresh promises that mandated individual quotas would be honoured.

Such alleged violators as Venezuela and Nigeria, who were said by sources in other delegations to have confessed, under Saudi Arabian and Iranian pressure, to over-producing were back in the lobbies on Thursday reiterating public denials.
"It is a lie," said Erwin Arrieta, Venezuela's minister.
The OPEC accord puts a ceiling on OPEC volume at 25.03 million barrels daily, including Iraq's sales under its food-for-oil deal with the United Nations.
But Western industry monitors say that violations of individual quotas have taken actual supply to 27 million.
Prices have sagged, from $25 in January, vexing Iran in particular, and apparently also irritating OPEC linchpin and Iran's fellow Gulf heavyweight and political rival Saudi Arabia.
Acccording to a Gulf source late on Wednesday, Venezuela admitted excess of 800,000 barrels or 30 percent above its quota during a candid session of ministerial talks.

"What is new is the complete honesty. All of the cheaters made confessions," said this source. But besides Venezuela, Nigeria on Thursday morning was also again insisting that it was not breaking quota.
Nigeria's Dan Etete blamed Western monitors. They had wrongly counted natural gas condensate as crude oil in their arithmetic, he said.
Among OPEC-watchers, John Lichtblau, head of Petroleum Industry Research Associates, deemed it "unthinkable" that populous, cash-pinched Third World sellers could cut to quota.
But a conference communique said the 11 members "made an undertaking to restrain output to their agreed level".
The secretary-general, Rilwanu Lukman, told a news conference that he was confident that efforts would be made to rein in production.
There was a general understanding that there had been "deviation", he said, but the impact of output cuts on the market was expected "fairly soon".
OPEC's outgoing Libyan president, Abdullah al-Badri, in a formal speech lamented the damage done by weak oil prices to the exporters' revenues.
He noted that prices had begun 1997 firmly.
But "the hard fact is that this general mood of optimism faded away...with the risk of bringing OPEC members' revenues and economies once again to a dangerously low level", he said.
-- Vienna newsroom +431 713 2002
